Empirical Research Plan: Effects of Educational Interventions on Student Achievement  

───────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
I will use a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences (DiD) design, estimated with modern two-way-fixed-effects–compatible estimators (e.g., Callaway-Sant’Anna or Sun-Abraham) and an event-study specification.  

Why it fits this setting  
• The reform was rolled out across schools at different calendar years while all students were repeatedly tested.  
• This creates plausibly exogenous variation in the timing of treatment, allowing students in not-yet-treated schools to serve as contemporaneous controls for students in already-treated schools.  
• Staggered DiD exploits both cross-sectional (treated vs. untreated) and time-series (before vs. after) variation to net out common shocks.  
• Modern estimators avoid the bias of traditional TWFE under treatment effect heterogeneity and produce cohort-specific and dynamic treatment effects that map directly into “short-run” vs. “long-run” effects.  

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
treated_it = 1 if student i attends a school that has implemented the intervention by year t; 0 otherwise.  
(We will also code first_treat_s = first school-year of implementation to build event-time dummies.)  

Control group (counterfactual)  
• Never-treated schools (if any) and not-yet-treated schools in years prior to adoption.  
• Students in these schools provide the counterfactual trajectory of test scores absent the intervention.  

Treatment timing / key variation  
• Variation: first_treat_s, the calendar year in which school s adopted the new program.  
• Exposure length: event_time = t – first_treat_s (…–2, –1, 0, +1, +2, …).  
Short-run = event_time 0/1; long-run = event_time ≥ 3 (choice can be adjusted).  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends conditional on controls  
In the absence of the intervention, outcome trends for treated schools would have paralleled those of control schools.  
Plausibility: Rollout was driven by administrative capacity, not measured achievement, suggesting no strong pre-trend differences; we will test for pre-trend equality.  

A2. No anticipatory effects  
Students/teachers do not change behavior before official implementation.  
Plausibility: The new curriculum requires formal training/materials delivered only at rollout; early behavioral changes likely small. Pre-treatment leads in the event study will be inspected.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-school spillovers)  
Spillovers across schools are minimal (different catchment areas).  
Plausibility: Geographic separation and school-specific curricula reduce spillovers, but we will probe robustness by dropping neighboring schools.  

A4. Stable composition  
Student attrition or in-migration is not differentially affected by treatment in a way correlated with potential outcomes.  
Plausibility: District assignment rules limit massive compositional shifts; we will verify balance in cohort size and demographics over time.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

Threat 1: Endogenous rollout (schools with rising scores adopt earlier).  
• Mitigation:  
  – Test for differential pre-trends in test scores and demographics.  
  – Add school-specific linear time trends as robustness.  
  – Instrumental-variables robustness: use policy-driven eligibility (e.g., funding waves) if available.  

Threat 2: Differential student mobility or attrition.  
• Mitigation:  
  – Track individual student IDs across schools; include origin-school-by-year fixed effects.  
  – Estimate effects on movers and stayers separately; re-weight to original composition (inverse-probability weights).  

Threat 3: Spillovers/spatial contamination.  
• Mitigation:  
  – Exclude schools within X miles of early adopters.  
  – Cluster standard errors at the school or district level.  

5. R Code Outline (executable)  

```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)         # fast data handling
library(fixest)             # Sun & Abraham TWFE
library(did)                # Callaway & Sant'Anna
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("student_intervention.csv")   # assumes columns: student_id, school_id,
                                          # year, test_score, intervention,
                                          # gender, race, ses, etc.

# 2. Construct treatment timing variables ------------------------------------
setorder(dt, school_id, year)

# first year the school implements
dt[, first_treat := year[intervention == 1][1], by = school_id]
dt[, ever_treated := !is.na(first_treat)]
dt[!ever_treated, first_treat := 0]      # code 0 for never-treated (per CS notation)

# event time (needed for Sun-Abraham event study)
dt[, event_time := ifelse(ever_treated, year - first_treat, -999)]

# Callaway-Sant’Anna group/period identifiers
dt[, G := first_treat]                   # group = cohort’s first treated year (0 = never)

# 3. Main specification: Callaway-Sant’Anna ATT ------------------------------
att_gt <- att_gt(yname   = "test_score",
                 tname   = "year",
                 idname  = "student_id",
                 gname   = "G",
                 xformla = ~ gender + race + ses,
                 data    = dt,
                 clustervars = "school_id")

agg_effect <- aggte(att_gt, type = "dynamic")  # event-study style
summary(agg_effect)
ggdid(agg_effect)                              # plot dynamic path

# 4. Robustness: Sun & Abraham TWFE ------------------------------------------
sa_mod <- feols(test_score ~ sunab(first_treat, year) +
                             gender + race + ses |
                             student_id + year,
                cluster = ~school_id,
                data = dt)
summary(sa_mod, agg = "att")        # automatically aggregates to overall ATT

# 5. Placebo pre-trend test ---------------------------------------------------
# Pre-treatment leads (-4 to -1) aggregated
iplot(sa_mod)

# 6. Additional robustness: school-specific trends ---------------------------
sa_trend <- feols(test_score ~ sunab(first_treat, year) +
                               gender + race + ses |
                               student_id + year + school_id[trend],
                  cluster = ~school_id, data = dt)
summary(sa_trend, agg = "att")
```

6. Expected Results  

Economic/educational theory predicts improved learning from enhanced pedagogy. I expect:  
• Short-run (1 year after rollout): +0.15 σ in standardized test scores.  
• Medium/long-run (3–5 years): gains may accumulate to roughly +0.25 σ.  
Magnitude calibrates to effects seen in high-quality tutoring or curriculum reforms in the literature.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = weak)  
Parallel trends evidence (pre-trend flat) ................. 0.8  
Exogeneity of rollout timing ............................... 0.7  
No interference/spillovers ................................ 0.6  
Stable composition / attrition ............................ 0.7  
Correct estimator for staggered timing .................... 1.0  

Overall, the design is strong but rests mainly on conditional parallel trends and non-endogenous adoption, both of which will be scrutinized through diagnostics and robustness checks.
